title: required members and MaybeNull / NotNull (analysis attributes)
hook: `required` forces callers to set a property in an object initializer — it does not forbid null. MaybeNull and NotNull teach the compiler contracts that generic signatures cannot spell.

blocks.text: Two complementary tools extend what NRT can express. The **`required` modifier** (C# 11+) says “whoever creates this object must assign this member in an initializer.” **Nullable analysis attributes** in `System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis` — `MaybeNull`, `NotNull`, `NotNullWhen`, and others — describe patterns like TryGetValue where a bool return tells you whether an out parameter is safe. Both change compiler warnings, not Intermediate Language (IL).

entries.plainDefinition: Forces object initializers (and constructors that do not opt out) to set the marked property or field.
Marks that a method may return null/default even when the return type annotation says otherwise — common on generic Find methods.
Says an out/ref parameter is not-null when the method returns true (or false, per argument).
Says a return value is not-null when a named parameter is not-null — dependent nullability the compiler can track.
On a constructor, disables required-member checks for that construction path. Use sparingly.
entries.example: Factory constructors that populate all required fields internally.

blocks.text: Generic APIs cannot always use `T?` cleanly — on structs it means `Nullable<T>`, on classes it means nullable annotation. Attributes document the *bool-returning* and *generic* patterns BCL types use everywhere: `TryParse`, `TryGetValue`, `IsNullOrEmpty`. Auth options classes use `required` so JWT issuer and audience cannot be forgotten at construction — but you still pick non-nullable types when null is invalid.

blocks.title: required vs non-null
blocks.body: `required string Audience` — caller must write the property; value should not be null. `required string? Optional` — caller must write the property; value *can* be null. Initialization ≠ presence.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Return bool for success
items.body: Separate “found” from the value. Callers must check the bool before using the out parameter.

items.title: Annotate the out parameter
items.body: `[NotNullWhen(true)]` on the out parameter tells the compiler: after true, it is safe to dereference.

items.title: Use MaybeNull on generic returns
items.body: When returning `T` from Find, mark `[return: MaybeNull]` so callers know a miss can happen.

items.title: Combine required with non-nullable types
items.body: For config records, `required string Connection` forces initialization with a not-null intent.

diagram.title: Attribute contracts in flow analysis
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  CALL[Call TryGet key out value] --> RET{Returns true?}
  RET -->|yes| NN[NotNullWhen: value is not-null]
  RET -->|no| MN[MaybeNullWhen: value maybe-null]
  NN --> USE[Safe to use value]
  MN --> SKIP[Do not dereference value]

snippet.label: Auth options with required plus NotNullWhen
snippet.explanation: Lines 3–4: `required` — omitting Issuer/Audience is a compile error. Line 5: optional claim stays `string?`. Lines 12–18: `NotNullWhen(true)` lets callers use `token` without `!` after a true return.

snippet.label: Generic cache TryGet with MaybeNullWhen
snippet.explanation: Line 1: `MaybeNullWhen(false)` — when TryGet returns false, `value` is maybe-null/default. Lines 3–6: on miss, return false and leave value unset. Line 8: on hit, cast and return true.

snippet.label: NotNullIfNotNull for dependent return contracts
snippet.explanation: Line 3: `[return: NotNullIfNotNull(nameof(key))]` — when `key` is not null, the return is treated as not-null if the method returns non-null. Models cache lookups where null key means null result but a real key implies a real payload when found.

snippet.label: Find with MaybeNull return
snippet.explanation: Line 1: `[return: MaybeNull]` documents that miss returns default/null. Lines 8–9: pattern match narrows before using nested properties.

blocks.title: Definite assignment patterns
rows: No keyword — convention or constructor params only

blocks.title: Believing required forbids null
blocks.body: `required string? name` means the caller must assign the property — even to null. Combine `required` with a non-nullable type when null is invalid.

blocks.title: Returning T from Find without MaybeNull
blocks.body: Callers will assume a miss is a valid object. Annotate the return or switch to `TryFind` with `[NotNullWhen(true)]`.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: nullable analysis attributes are compile-time contracts only — no IL change. `[NotNullIfNotNull(nameof(param))]` on returns models dependent nullability: null in implies null out allowed; non-null in raises the bar on the return. BCL uses `[NotNullWhen(true)]` on TryGetValue out parameters. Generic `T?` is ambiguous on unconstrained T — prefer MaybeNull, NotNull, MemberNotNullWhen on library APIs. required enforces presence in initializers, not non-null — pair with non-nullable types for auth Issuer/Audience fields.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Options, DTOs — not same as non-null

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying required forbids null. Returning T from Find without MaybeNull. Not knowing NotNullIfNotNull for dependent returns. Sprinkling null! instead of attributes on generic Try APIs.

interviewTakeaways: required enforces initialization — not non-null unless the type is non-nullable.
NotNullWhen, MaybeNull, NotNullIfNotNull refine generic and bool-returning contracts.
Attributes change warnings only — validate at process boundaries anyway.
60s: required is presence in initializer. NotNullWhen for Try*. MaybeNull on Find. NotNullIfNotNull when return tracks argument null. No runtime enforcement.
Follow-up: why is T? awkward on unconstrained generic T?
commonPitfalls: Saying required means non-null gets you rejected.
Find<T> without MaybeNull — callers assume hit.
Strong answer: 'required is init presence. NotNullWhen for Try. NotNullIfNotNull for dependent returns. Attributes are analysis only.'

jsTsCorrelations.concept: definite assignment and definite assignment assertions
jsTsCorrelations.note: TypeScript definite assignment (`!`) on fields is a cousin to C# `required` and field-level `null!`. `required` is a language error; TS `!` is an assertion.
